newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Montserrat volcano expels heavy ash cloud.
newsitem.headline: Montserrat volcano expels heavy ash cloud.

text.p: The Soufriere Hills volcano belched more rock and hot gases on Wednesday, sending a shower of ash 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) into the air.

Scientists at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory advised residents of this British Caribbean colony to wear masks outdoors to protect against the swirling clouds of dust from the rumbling volcano. Rivers of superheated rock and gas this week breached the south wall and rolled down its southern flank for the first time.

The heavy ashfall temporarily closed Plymouth's port -- considered a key to maintaining the island's fragile economy -- but the island's rice mill and power plant remained open, Franklyn Michael, director of Montserrat's emergency operations centre, said.
Authorities advised residents to limit visits to the abandoned capital and carry transistor radios at all times to listen for warnings in case of major rock flows.

"It generated some very large ash clouds that reached quite far north, all the way to St. John's, one of the northernmost towns," Michael said. "We have experienced ashfall that is considerably heavier than what we are used to."

The activity in the volatile mountain came nearly a year after the last evacuation of Montserrat's southern end. On April 3, 1996, about 4,000 residents were moved from the capital and towns in the south to northern "safe zones."
The April evacuation, which is still in effect, was the third since the mountain awakened in July 1995 following nearly four centuries of volcanic dormancy.
A portion of Galway's Wall at the volcano's peak collapsed on Monday, allowing flows of rock and hot gases down the White River Valley which obliterated the Great Alp waterfall, a tourist attraction.
